title: Job Scheduler
description: Design a distributed job scheduler — one-off and recurring jobs, executing within seconds of their scheduled time, at-least-once delivery, retries and status tracking.
author: Editorial Team

blocks.title: What is a Job Scheduler?
blocks.text: A job scheduler runs tasks at a specified time or on a recurring schedule — "send this email in 2 hours", "rebuild the report every night at 2am" — across a fleet of workers.

items: Users should be able to schedule a job to run immediately, at a future time, or on a recurring (cron) schedule.
Users should be able to monitor the status of their jobs (pending, running, succeeded, failed).
Cancelling or editing jobs after creation.

blocks.question: What are the non-functional requirements for this system?

items: Jobs should start within ~2 seconds of their scheduled time.
The system should be highly available and never silently drop a job (at-least-once execution).
It should scale to 10,000 job executions per second.
Jobs can fail; the system should retry them with backoff.
Exactly-once execution guarantees (jobs should be idempotent).

lines: - schedule job: now / at time / cron
blocks.caption: Job Scheduler Requirements

blocks.text: The key modelling insight is to separate the **job definition** (what to run and its schedule) from each **execution** (one concrete run at one time). Recurring jobs produce many executions.

items: **Job**: the task definition — type, parameters, and schedule (one-off time or cron expression).
**Execution**: one scheduled run of a job — execution time, status, attempt count.

blocks.text: 1) Users should be able to schedule jobs

A **Job Service** validates the request and writes a Job row, then writes the first Execution row with its `scheduledAt` time and status `PENDING`. For recurring jobs, the next execution is created when the current one is picked up.
2) Executions should run at their scheduled time
A **Watcher** periodically queries for executions that are due and pushes them onto a queue; **Workers** consume from the queue and run them.
3) Users should be able to monitor their jobs
Workers update the Execution status as they progress. The status API reads executions by `jobId` (and by user), so we index Executions on `(jobId, scheduledAt)`.
1) How do we start jobs within 2 seconds of their scheduled time?

blocks.title: Poll the database every few seconds for due jobs

approach.text: The Watcher runs `SELECT * FROM executions WHERE scheduled_at <= now() AND status = 'PENDING'` every couple of seconds.

challenges.text: At 10k executions per second this is a heavy, constant query on the primary database, and frequent polling still adds up to the poll interval of delay.

blocks.title: Two-tier scheduling: DB for the long term, delayed queue for the near term

approach.text: Query the database only every few minutes for executions due in the **next window** (say 5 minutes) and enqueue them into a queue that supports per-message delivery delays (e.g. SQS delay seconds, or a Redis sorted set scored by time). The queue releases each message at its exact time, so workers see it within milliseconds. Jobs created for "now" or within the current window skip the database scan and go straight to the delayed queue.

challenges.text: The window boundary needs care so jobs aren't missed or double-enqueued — enqueueing is idempotent by execution ID, and status moves from `PENDING` to `QUEUED` with a conditional update.

blocks.text: 2) How do we make sure no job is ever dropped?

blocks.title: Workers mark status in the database

approach.text: Workers set status to `RUNNING` when they start and `SUCCEEDED` when they finish.

challenges.text: If a worker crashes mid-job, the execution is stuck in `RUNNING` forever.

approach.text: Workers receive messages with a **visibility timeout**: if they don't acknowledge in time (because they crashed), the queue redelivers the message to another worker. Long jobs extend the timeout with heartbeats. Failures are retried with exponential backoff up to a max attempt count, after which the execution goes to a dead-letter queue and is marked `FAILED`.

challenges.text: This is at-least-once delivery, so a job may run twice (e.g. a worker finishes but crashes before acking). Jobs must be **idempotent** — pass an idempotency key (the execution ID) to downstream systems.

blocks.title: Pattern: Managing Long Running Tasks
blocks.text: Decoupling submission from execution with a durable queue and tracking status separately is the core of this pattern.
3) How do we scale to 10k executions per second?

Partition the Executions table by time bucket (e.g. hourly) so the scheduler only touches the hot partition, and keep historical executions in cheaper storage. Run multiple Watchers that each own a shard of jobs (by `hash(jobId)`), coordinated via leases so two watchers never scan the same shard. Workers scale horizontally on queue depth.

quiz.question: Why model Job and Execution as separate entities?
options: A recurring job produces many independent executions with their own status
quiz.explanation: Each run has its own time, attempts and status; the job only defines what and when.

quiz.question: What ensures a job is retried if its worker crashes?
options: The queue's visibility timeout redelivers unacknowledged messages
quiz.explanation: Unacked messages become visible again after the timeout and are picked up by another worker.

quiz.question: With at-least-once delivery, what property must jobs have?
quiz.explanation: A job may run more than once; idempotent jobs make duplicates harmless.

quiz.question: How does the two-tier design achieve ~2s precision without hammering the database?
options: Scanning the DB occasionally for the next window and using a delayed queue for exact timing
quiz.explanation: The DB is scanned every few minutes; the delayed queue releases each message at its precise time.
